1:
One lot falls to two tribes, and Keil (grammatical-historical) explains it: the sons of Joseph drew together so that Manasseh’s half should not be cut off from Ephraim, and the territory was divided immediately after, Ephraim taking the southern part and Manasseh the northern. That is why the southern boundary of the whole is described first, marked off against Benjamin and Dan, before the chapter turns to Ephraim. Gill (reformed) notes that the phrase is went out, of the urn, this being the next lot after Judah’s, the government belonging to Judah and the birthright to Joseph. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds why the two are named as one here and separately later: these verses speak of them together.

Henry (puritan-evangelical) accounts for the favour shown. Joseph was a younger son but the eldest by Rachel, and had kept the family from perishing in the famine; so his posterity were well served, their portion lying in the heart of Canaan and running its whole breadth, with a fruitfulness answering the blessings of Genesis 49:25 and Deuteronomy 33:13. He then notices what the chapter omits: these tribes get boundaries but no list of cities, unlike Judah before and the rest after; and Henry can assign no reason unless Joshua, being himself of the children of Joseph, allotted their towns himself, so the names never went before the council. Calvin (reformed) is struck by a related oddity: more words are spent on the remaining half of Manasseh than on the whole of Ephraim, though Ephraim was more populous and had the better claim to space. His answer is that Manasseh needed the extra detail — the settlement in Bashan given without a lot, and the ratification of Moses’ ruling about Zelophehad’s daughters — whereas Ephraim’s bounds admitted no dispute. He raises a further question and answers it himself: if the birthright had passed to Ephraim, how did Ephraim come to hold cities inside Manasseh’s territory, which looks like the inferior position? Because, he says, Manasseh’s portion outran its numbers, and towns were deducted to bring Ephraim to its just share.

The border begins at a puzzle. Gill holds that Bethel and Luz, though they later became one, were originally distinct, Bethel a field adjacent to the city. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) agrees they seem distinct here while conceding that Genesis 28:19 identifies them, and suggests the place of Jacob’s vision lay near Luz rather than in it, so the whole was called sometimes by one name and sometimes the other — as London takes in Westminster and Southwark, though all three can be named apart. Keil resolves it more precisely: what is meant is not the town but the southern hills belonging to Bethel, from which the line ran out to Luz, which stood on the border and fell to Benjamin.

The rest of the line is a string of places, and the two who chase them use different instruments. Clarke measures from Jerusalem, putting Ataroth at fifteen miles and lower Beth-horon at twelve, toward the town later called Emmaus, and glosses Ataroth-addar as Ataroth the illustrious. Keil works on the ground, naming lower Beth-horon as a village on a low ridge cut off from the upper town by a deep wady, and correcting an identification of Ataroth he had once accepted himself, replacing it with ruins further south. On one name they converge: the Arkite of the boundary is otherwise unknown, and both fix him by the one descendant Scripture records, David’s friend Hushai the Archite at 2 Samuel 15:32. On another they agree in defeat. Keil says the Japhletite is altogether unknown and cannot be the Asherite of that name; Gill says the place is now unknown, and adds the observation that redeems the list — it was clear enough to the sons of Joseph when the lot fell.
5:
Keil (grammatical-historical) sets out the shape of the description: the southern line is repeated in brief, then the northern boundary traced from a central point near the watershed, first east and then west. He notices that the upper Beth-horon is named where the earlier passage had the lower, and says it makes no difference, the two standing close together; Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says the same, that its situation is little known but lay east of the nether and near it. Gill (reformed) marks the point where the general lot ends and Ephraim’s own border begins, and Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) corrects the compass, reading the east side as the north-east.

Three witnesses then say the same thing about the whole exercise, and it is the honest note of the chapter. Henry (puritan-evangelical) reports that the learned who try to draw the line exactly find themselves much at a loss, and that modern travellers cannot clear it, the country being so unlike what it was: cities destroyed until no footstep remains, brooks dried up, rivers gone out of their courses, and, as Job 14:18 has it, the rock removed out of his place. Rather than list doubts he cannot settle, he declines to raise them, observing that the border was perfectly understood at the time, so the purpose of recording it was answered. Wesley says it is no wonder some of this is dark at such a distance, and rests on the same certainty, that every description here was evident to the Israelites, being the foundation of possessions they held peaceably for ages after. Gill had already put it in a phrase, that a place now unknown was well known to the men whose lot it bounded.

What that costs in practice is visible in the identifications. Keil finds a second Ataroth here, places it by the word went down on the eastern slope above the Ghor, and admits it has not been discovered; Gill also takes it for a different Ataroth, there being several of the name, but puts it four miles from Samaria, another region altogether. Naarath Keil identifies from an old gazetteer that sets it five Roman miles from Jericho. On Jericho itself he and Wesley agree exactly: the line touched the district and not the city, which belonged to Benjamin. Tappuah divides them. Clarke calls it a city of Manasseh that gave its name to a district; Keil argues it cannot be the royal town of that name, since a boundary running there would go south to north instead of westward, and rejects a second proposal on the same ground, concluding that the place lay west of Shechem and has not been found. Gill only distinguishes it from the Tappuah of Judah.

The survey ends with towns outside the lines drawn. Gill and Wesley explain them the same way: Ephraim was much the larger tribe, so besides the territory its boundaries marked it received separate cities inside Manasseh’s portion, with their villages. Clarke puts it as a transfer, cities separated from Manasseh and given to Ephraim. Keil reports the reason Calvin gives — that comparing each territory with the numbers holding it left Ephraim too little — allows it as possible, then qualifies it: other reasons may lie beyond recovery, since the same arrangement appears in Manasseh’s case at Joshua 17. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the arrangement as designed. Interlocking holdings gave the tribes common interests and made disunion harder, the stronger having a stake in completing the conquest of the weaker’s ground; and he compares the Roman testudo, where each man’s shield covered part of his own body and part of his neighbour’s, so that no missile could get through. So the tribes, he says, were built as a city compact together, joined so that if one member suffered the rest must suffer with it.
10:
The chapter closes on a failure, and the witnesses divide over whether it was inability or unwillingness. Keil (grammatical-historical) states it flatly as the first: from Gezer they could not drive the Canaanites out, so these remained among the Ephraimites in a state of serfdom, and the notice is to be read exactly like the parallel about Judah at Joshua 15:63, which Ellicott (grammatical-historical) also sets beside it. Gill (reformed) leaves the question open and lists three possibilities: that they could not, God withholding the victory because of their sins; that they were slothful; or that covetousness kept them, since a trading people might be unwilling to lose the profit of such neighbours — which he thinks the clause about tribute hints at. Henry (puritan-evangelical) will not allow inability at all and calls the verse a brand on the tribe: carelessness or cowardice, want of faith in a promise that would have carried a vigorous effort through, or want of zeal for a command that obliged them to drive the Canaanites out utterly and make no peace with them. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) splits the difference in four words, saying they could not, or at least did not.

The tribute itself is then weighed. Henry reports Calvin (reformed) as holding that putting the Canaanites under tribute made the matter worse rather than better: it shows the sparing was for covetousness, to profit by their labour, and the dealing that followed exposed Israel to their idolatry. Henry records the kinder reading too, that in taking tribute they required the Canaanites to renounce their idols and keep the precepts given to the sons of Noah — and then abandons it, because the sequel of the story shows Israel so far from restraining idolatry in others that they soon fell into it themselves. Clarke observes how long the failure lasted: the Canaanites were not cleared from Gezer until the days of Solomon, and then not by Israel at all, the city being taken by the king of Egypt and given to his daughter as a wedding gift at 1 Kings 9:16. He allows that Ephraim had at least subdued them far enough to exact tribute, but not far enough to expel them.

Clarke ends the chapter on the difficulty that has run through it. Many of these towns were small and slightly built, and may have perished a thousand years ago and more, so that it is useless to look for them now. He answers the obvious objection with an argument from home: towns in England, a country never exposed to such revolutions as Palestine, are named by Caesar and other ancient writers and can no longer be found; several have changed their names and not a few their sites, Norwich being said to have stood some miles from where it now stands, and Salisbury demonstrably so. Such changes, he concludes, do not affect the truth of the ancient geography of his own country, and cannot impeach the geography of the historian before him. It is the same point Gill, Henry and Wesley make earlier in the chapter, argued the other way round: not that the places were plain to those who used them, but that their disappearance since proves nothing against the record.
